hints: Look closely at Fig. 5.1. The cat shows long hair and pointed pattern. Both traits are described as recessive - what does that tell you about the alleles it must carry?
A recessive phenotype can only appear when no dominant allele is present. Translate long hair and pointed into symbols using h and r.
The other parent is heterozygous for both genes. Think about how many different gamete combinations independent assortment can make from HhRr.
The Fig. 5.1 cat can only make one type of gamete. Pair that single gamete type with each of the four gamete types from the heterozygous parent.
To get phenotypes, check each F1 genotype for the presence of H and R. Any H gives short hair, any R gives full colour.
walkthrough:
Work Out The Fig. 5.1 Cat**
You are sitting with a long-haired, pointed cat. Short hair $H$ is dominant to long hair $h$, and full colour $R$ is dominant to pointed $r$. A recessive trait only shows when the dominant allele is absent, so long hair must be $hh$ and pointed must be $rr$. That makes this parent $hhrr$ with phenotype long hair pointed.

Work Out The Second Parent**
The second cat looks dominant for both traits but is heterozygous for both. That means one dominant and one recessive allele at each locus: $HhRr$ with phenotype short hair full colour. This is effectively a dihybrid test cross.

Write The Gametes Using Independent Assortment**
Because the genes are unlinked they assort independently in meiosis. The $hhrr$ parent can only make $hr$ gametes. The $HhRr$ parent can make four equal types: $HR$, $Hr$, $hR$, $hr$.

Combine To Get F1 Genotypes**
Join the single $hr$ with each of the four types: $hr \times HR$ gives $HhRr$, $hr \times Hr$ gives $Hhrr$, $hr \times hR$ gives $hhRr$, $hr \times hr$ gives $hhrr$. All four are expected in equal proportions.

Translate Genotypes Into Phenotypes**
Any genotype with $H$ is short hair, $hh$ is long hair. Any genotype with $R$ is full colour, $rr$ is pointed. So $HhRr$ is short hair full colour, $Hhrr$ is short hair pointed, $hhRr$ is long hair full colour, $hhrr$ is long hair pointed.

Final answer: parent phenotypes: long hair pointed x short hair full colour; parent genotypes: $hhrr \times HhRr$; gametes: $hr$ from $hhrr$ and $HR$, $Hr$, $hR$, $hr$ from $HhRr$; F1 genotypes: $HhRr$, $Hhrr$, $hhRr$, $hhrr$; F1 phenotypes: short hair full colour, short hair pointed, long hair full colour, long hair pointed in 1:1:1:1 ratio.

hints: Scan Fig. 5.2 for a family where the offspring shows a trait neither parent shows in full. Focus on the full colour x full colour pair on the right middle and their son.
walkthrough:
Spot The Hidden Trait**
If pointed were dominant, at least one parent of every pointed cat would have to be pointed. Look at the pair in the middle-right: a full colour female $-/+$ $4/6$ crossed with a full colour male $-/+$ $4/7$ have a pointed son $-/-$ $3/4$.

Explain Why This Proves Recessive**
Two full colour parents can only have a pointed kitten if they both carry a hidden pointed allele $r$ and pass $r$ and $r$ on. The pointed kitten is $rr$ with no $Hpa$II site ($-/-$). This is the classic recessive pattern.
Final answer: Two full colour parents produce a pointed offspring, so pointed must be recessive and carried hidden in heterozygotes.

hints: Think about what is different for a gene on the X chromosome. How many alleles would a male cat have, and from which parent must he get his X?
Look at the numbers under each cat in Fig. 5.2. Check whether sons ever receive a marker allele from their father, and whether sons always match their mother for colour.
walkthrough:
Rule Out X-Linkage Using Male Genotypes**
For an X-linked gene males are hemizygous and would show only one allele. Every male in Fig. 5.2 shows two marker alleles, for example the top-left male is $-/-$ $2/4$ and the middle male is $-/-$ $2/4$. Males clearly carry two copies, as expected for an autosome.

Use Father-To-Son Transmission**
If the gene were on the X, a son gets his X only from his mother and nothing from his father. Here sons clearly get one marker number from the father. For example the top cross $2/4 \times 3/4$ gives daughter $2/4$ and son $2/4$, and the full colour father $6/7$ passes 6 to his daughter and 7 to his son. Coat colour of sons is also not determined by the mother alone, confirming autosomal inheritance.

Final answer: Autosomal because males show two marker alleles, e.g. $4/7$, so have two copies; sons receive one marker allele from the father, e.g. father $6/7$ gives 6 or 7 to offspring, which is impossible for X-linkage where sons get X only from mother.

hints: If two loci are close together on the same chromosome they travel as a block. Check whether a particular + or - always stays with the same marker number, e.g. follow 6, 7, 4 and 2 through the pedigree.
Look for any break in that pattern that would show crossing over. Does any cat show a new combination of + / - with a marker number not seen in its parents?
walkthrough:
Follow The Blocks Through The Pedigree**
Think of each chromosome as carrying a pair: restriction status plus marker number. The full colour grandfather $+/+$ $6/7$ passes $+6$ to his daughter and $+7$ to his son. The pointed grandmother $-/-$ $3/4$ passes $-4$ on. In the next generation $-/+$ $4/6$ and $-/+$ $4/7$ keep those same pairs intact.

Note The Lack Of Recombination**
If the marker were far from $R/r$, crossing over would shuffle + and - onto different numbers and you would see new combinations. No new combinations appear. Every offspring combination can be explained without recombination, so the marker locus must lie very close to $R/r$ and be closely linked.
Final answer: Plus / minus and marker number are inherited together as a block with no recombination seen, e.g. $+6$, $+7$ and $-4$, $-2$ conserved through generations.
